dek.text: USDA uses AI models to pick where Texas surveils, traps and releases sterile flies against New World screwworm. Its own scientists say the models miss one thing.

introduction.text: [The U.S. Department of Agriculture uses predictive models built with artificial intelligence to choose where, when and how many sterile flies to release against New World screwworm](c2). [The fly lays its eggs in open wounds and body openings](c23). [Those eggs hatch into maggots that feed on living tissue](c24).

[Kim Lohmeyer directs the research service's livestock insects laboratory in Kerrville](c6). [Lohmeyer says the models already pick areas for surveillance, adult fly trapping and sterile fly releases](c4). [Lohmeyer also says they can't predict every scenario, especially people transporting infested animals](c5).

paragraphs.text: [The Texas Animal Health Commission says the fly was first confirmed in Texas on {{date:c26}} in a calf in Zavala County](c26). [That calf has recovered and its case is considered inactive](c34).

[The commission now counts {{number:c28}} Texas premises with at least one confirmed detection](c28). [Those premises sit in {{number:c27}} counties](c27). [Movement restrictions cover an established infested zone in parts of counties that run from Brewster and Presidio to Starr and Zapata](c29).

[The research service says its models read ecological and environmental records to predict where the pest is likely to become established and how it may spread](c1). [The system is meant to send aircraft, personnel, fly traps and sterile insects where they protect the most](c3).

[USDA says its Edinburg facility deploys more than {{number:c19:1}} million sterile flies a week](c19). [An agency page says the facility can disperse up to {{number:c20}} million a week](c20). [A production plant planned for South Texas is projected at {{number:c21}} million a week](c21).
[The sterile insect technique helped eradicate the fly from the United States in {{number:c25}}](c25). [It also ended a small Florida Keys outbreak in {{number:c25:1}}](c25).

[KRGV reported that USDA has flown drones across Texas more than {{number:c10}} times since June](c10). [The agency said it observed more than {{number:c11}} animals and found no screwworm case among them](c11). That result covers the animals the drones saw and says nothing about the premises the commission has confirmed.
[USDA officials also told KRGV the drones are not foolproof for detecting screwworm](c12).

[Lohmeyer names one blind spot above the rest, people moving infested animals](c5). [The research service tells livestock owners never to move an animal that shows signs of infestation or is suspected of it](c9).

[The commission says a suspected case should be reported within {{number:c30}} hours of suspicion](c30). [Reports go to a regional office or to its veterinarian on call](c31). Whether the models will ever account for animals moved by hand is a question the published material does not answer.
